hints: Think about where each scale lives: the stage micrometer sits on the stage like a tiny ruler slide, while the eyepiece graticule sits in the eyepiece. Which one stays in place when you look at your cell specimen?

Remember the two jobs in calibration: one scale has a known true value in micrometres, the other has arbitrary eyepiece units. Also ask yourself what happens to field of view when you go from $\times10$ to $\times40$ objective.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two different scales**

Think of the stage micrometer as a very tiny, accurate ruler placed on the stage. It is usually $1 \text{ mm}$ divided into 100 divisions, so each division = $10 \mu\text{m}$.

Think of the eyepiece graticule as a transparent scale in the eyepiece with arbitrary units. It stays in your view and is what you actually use to measure cells.

**Check statements 1 and 2**

Statement 1 is not correct. You do not leave the stage micrometer under the microscope to measure cells. You remove it and put your specimen slide on instead.

Statement 2 is correct. The whole point of the stage micrometer is calibration. You line up the two scales to work out what one eyepiece unit equals in $\mu\text{m}$ at that magnification.

**Check statement 3 and conclude**

Statement 3 is correct. Going from $\times10$ to $\times40$ objective gives higher magnification but a smaller field of view. So you see fewer divisions of the stage micrometer scale.

That gives us 2 and 3 only, which is option B.

options.A: Includes statement 1, which is false. The stage micrometer is removed after calibration and cells are measured with the calibrated eyepiece graticule.
options.B: Correct, statements 2 and 3 are true. The stage micrometer calibrates the eyepiece graticule, and higher magnification shows less of the scale.
options.C: Statement 1 alone is false. You cannot measure cells directly with the stage micrometer because it is not present when the specimen is viewed.
options.D: Statement 2 is true but this option misses statement 3, which is also true because field of view decreases at $\times40$.
